title: The job-ready playbook
subtitle: Help with your resume, projects, job search, and interviews, whether you are applying for your first role or changing jobs.

chapters.title: Choose the roles you want to apply for
chapters.label: Choosing a role
chapters.intro: Start by deciding what kind of work you want. That makes it easier to choose what to study and which experience to put on your resume.

sections.title: Read a few job descriptions
sections.text: Find five to ten openings that interest you. Compare the responsibilities and the skills that keep coming up. Check the experience level, location, and working arrangements too. Choose one main role and a closely related alternative. Use those titles in your job preferences when they describe the work you can do.

sections.title: Work out what you can already show
sections.text: For each common requirement, note a project, work task, or course exercise you could talk about. Put anything you have only watched in a video on your study list. Practise it until you can use it and explain how it works.

sections.title: Set an application target you can manage
sections.text: You could start with three relevant applications on a weekday. Adjust that around your studies and other commitments. Give a strong match enough time to read the description and prepare the application, then look at the responses each week.

example.label: Write down your target
example.text: I am looking for [role]. My most relevant work is [project or experience], where I [what you did].

checklist: Choose a main role and a related alternative
Read five job descriptions
Match the common requirements to work you can explain

chapters.title: Keep your profiles consistent
chapters.label: Resume and profiles
chapters.intro: Someone reading your resume, LinkedIn, GitHub, or portfolio should find the same facts about where you worked and what you did.

sections.title: Check the details across your profiles
sections.text: Compare your dates, job titles, employment types, education, and project names. You can give more detail on one platform than another. If a vendor employed you on a client assignment, name the employer and explain the client work accurately.

sections.title: Make your projects easy to review
sections.text: Write a short headline that describes the work you want to do. Pick two or three relevant projects to feature. For each one, explain the problem, the part you built, and a decision you made. Include enough evidence for someone to inspect the work. A repository README should explain how to run it and what its limits are.

sections.title: Use numbers you can explain
sections.text: For a result on your resume, know the baseline and how you measured the change. Say whether it came from a local test, a prototype, or production. If you recently joined a team, describe what you are building and what you have finished so far. Add results once you have measured them, and keep confidential employer data out of public profiles.

example.label: A project description you can adapt
example.text: I built [feature] to help with [problem]. I was responsible for [part of the work]. I chose [approach] because [reason], and checked it using [test or evaluation]. It still has [limitation].

checklist: Check dates and titles across your profiles
Feature projects that fit the roles you want
Check how each result was measured

chapters.title: Write a resume for your first job
chapters.label: For freshers
chapters.intro: If you have not had a formal job yet, use projects and other work you have done. Give the interviewer something you can show and discuss.

sections.title: Put the most useful information first
sections.text: Contact details, relevant skills, selected projects, education, and any genuine experience are a useful starting order. Move education higher if it is your strongest qualification. For an early-career resume, try a readable page first and use more space only if the content needs it.

sections.title: Explain your part in a project
sections.text: Describe the problem, what you implemented, the tools you used, and how you tested it. In a team project, say which part was yours. Add a repository or demo link where it helps, and open it in a signed-out browser to check that other people can access it.

sections.title: Describe experience honestly
sections.text: You can include academic projects, volunteering, freelance work, open-source contributions, and self-directed work. Label each for what it was. A virtual job simulation is different from employment. Only list internships and certificates you completed. Do not invent an employer, a certificate, dates, or results to fill a gap.

example.label: Project bullet
example.text: Implemented [feature] in [project] using [tools]. Checked [behaviour] with [tests or evaluation]. Use details from work you have done.

checklist: Choose projects you can run and explain
Describe your contribution to team work
Check every experience and credential you list

chapters.title: Describe your work experience clearly
chapters.label: For experienced applicants
chapters.intro: A recruiter needs to understand what you were responsible for and what you contributed. Give them more than a list of duties.

sections.title: Explain what you did
sections.text: Start a bullet with the action you took, explain the part you owned, and include an outcome if you have evidence for it. Make your contribution clear when the result belongs to a team. Give recent work that fits the new role more space.

sections.title: Be specific about ongoing work
sections.text: If you recently joined, describe the component you are building and its current stage. A completed design review, implemented validation, or added tests can be worth mentioning when that is what you did. Describe deployment and business results only once they have happened.

sections.title: Keep a record while the work is fresh
sections.text: Privately note the problem, your decisions, who you worked with, and results you are allowed to share. Keep technical measurements separate from business outcomes. For claims about latency or quality, record the baseline and relevant details such as the dataset, sample size, and hardware. Follow your employer's confidentiality rules.

example.label: An ongoing-work bullet
example.text: Implementing [component] for [use case]. Completed [milestone] and currently checking [specific behaviour].

checklist: Replace a vague duty with a specific contribution
Separate your work from a team-wide result
Check that ongoing work is described as ongoing

chapters.title: Understand the projects on your resume
chapters.label: Project preparation
chapters.intro: Choose a project that uses skills your target role needs. Finish a version you can run, then get comfortable explaining and changing it.

sections.title: Choose a manageable project
sections.text: Decide who it is for, which problem it solves, and what the first version needs to do. Include setup instructions, a short demo, and a README explaining the architecture and known limits. Two finished projects you understand are usually easier to discuss than several unfinished copies.

sections.title: Check the code you get from AI
sections.text: AI can help you build, explain unfamiliar code, or suggest tests and alternatives. Review what it produces, check dependencies and licences, and keep secrets out of the repository. Before you put the project on your resume, run it yourself. You should be able to change a feature, debug a failure, and explain the important design choices. Describe your contribution and any assistance accurately.

sections.title: Practise explaining it before you apply
sections.text: Give a two-minute walkthrough of the problem and the flow from input to output. Describe your part and one case where the project fails. Prepare to explain why you chose the approach, how you tested it, and what you would change next. Learn the main parts before applying, then revisit the details before an interview.

checklist: Run the project from a clean setup
Write down the architecture and its limits
Practise explaining a design choice and a failure case

chapters.title: Find jobs that fit your skills
chapters.label: Searching for jobs
chapters.intro: Read the description before applying. Spend your time on roles where you can explain how your skills or experience fit the work.

sections.title: Use a focused search
sections.text: Search for a role title with a skill you know. Try related titles, then filter for location, work arrangement, and experience. Date-posted filters can help you check recent openings, including the last 24 hours where that option is available. A recent post is worth checking, though it does not guarantee fewer applicants or a reply. [S2]

sections.title: Complete your Naukri and LinkedIn profiles
sections.text: Add accurate skills, experience, availability, and preferred titles and locations. Check recommended jobs and set up relevant alerts or saved searches. Update your profile when something changes. Changing a word every day is not a reliable way to get hired; use that time to review openings and apply to suitable ones. [S3]

sections.title: Check the company's careers page
sections.text: Keep a short list of companies you would like to work for. When possible, confirm an opening on the official careers page and follow its instructions. Check the main responsibilities, mandatory requirements, work eligibility, location, and seniority. You can apply without every preferred skill, but be honest about gaps that affect your ability to do the job. Save the job URL, description, date, and source in case the listing disappears.

checklist: Set accurate role and location preferences
Create an alert for a relevant search
Save suitable openings with their descriptions

chapters.title: Tailor your resume before applying
chapters.label: Preparing an application
chapters.intro: Make the experience that matters to this role easy to find. Keep the facts the same as you change the emphasis.

sections.title: Match the description to your work
sections.text: Read the full description and pick the projects or work examples that show you can handle the main responsibilities. Move relevant bullets higher. Use the employer's terms when they accurately describe skills you have. Keep a master resume and save the version you send for each role. Be ready to explain why the role fits you and which examples support that. [S1]

sections.title: Check the file you will send
sections.text: Use readable text, standard section headings, and a simple layout. Follow the requested file format. Check spelling and links after exporting, and make sure the text can be selected. Copying it into a plain text editor can reveal problems, although it cannot guarantee how every applicant tracking system will read the file.

sections.title: Check the application details
sections.text: Confirm the company and title, attach the correct resume, and answer screening questions truthfully. If a cover letter is requested, explain how one or two relevant examples fit the work. Record the date, resume version, and a follow-up reminder. Avoid submitting the same application twice. [S1]

example.label: An AI prompt for editing your resume
example.text: Compare this job description with my resume. Suggest which existing work to emphasise. Do not invent skills, experience, metrics, employers, or credentials. Point out requirements I have not demonstrated.

checklist: Choose evidence for the main requirements
Read the exported resume and test its links
Save the version you submit

chapters.title: Contact recruiters and ask for referrals
chapters.label: Messages and follow-ups
chapters.intro: Say which role you are asking about and why it interests you. Keep the request short enough that someone can answer it quickly.

sections.title: Use the contact details in the listing
sections.text: Use a recruiting email or professional channel published for the role. Include the title and reference number if there is one. Follow any contact instructions, avoid personal numbers, and do not send repeated messages. Share only what the application needs.

sections.title: Give a referral request some context
sections.text: Mention the opening and one example of relevant work. Ask whether the person is comfortable reviewing your fit or explaining the referral process. Give them room to decline. A referral still requires you to follow the company's application process.

sections.title: Allow time before following up
sections.text: Use the employer's timeline if they give one. Otherwise, roughly seven to ten business days is a reasonable starting point for a polite check-in. Include the role and when you applied, then ask about next steps. Keep applying elsewhere and respect any no-contact instruction.

example.label: Application follow-up
example.text: Hello [name], I applied for [role / reference] on [date]. My work on [example] involved [your contribution], which fits [requirement]. Could you share any update on the next steps? Thank you for your time.

checklist: Check that the contact channel is intended for applicants
Mention the role and one relevant example
Set a follow-up date based on the employer's timeline

chapters.title: Make time to study while you apply
chapters.label: Study and interview practice
chapters.intro: Pick a study window you can keep. Decide what you will work on before you sit down, and put distracting apps away.

sections.title: Give each session a clear task
sections.text: If you have two hours, try 45 minutes learning a concept, 45 minutes using it, 20 minutes explaining it without notes, and 10 minutes choosing the next task. Take breaks when you need them. Start with a shorter session if two hours does not fit your day, then increase it gradually.

sections.title: Check what you understood
sections.text: After a lesson, close it and explain the idea in your own words. Try an exercise or change the example. Note what you could not explain and ask a specific question about it. Watching a course to the end does not tell you whether you can use the material in an interview.

sections.title: Prepare for the interview you have
sections.text: Read the job description again, along with the resume you submitted and information about the company's product. Practise the fundamentals and practical tasks relevant to the role. Prepare a project walkthrough, examples of working with other people, and questions for the team. Check your interview setup and ask for any accessibility adjustments you need.

checklist: Choose a study time you can keep
Explain a concept without reading your notes
Practise a project walkthrough before the interview

chapters.title: Review your search each week
chapters.label: Your next two weeks
chapters.intro: Keep a record of applications and interviews so you can see where to make changes. A week with no replies gives you very little evidence on its own.

sections.title: Use the first week to prepare
sections.text: Choose your target roles, check your profiles, and prepare your resume. Finish a case study for one project and set up job alerts and an application tracker. Ask someone you trust to review one application against its job description.

sections.title: Apply and review the responses
sections.text: In the second week, apply to a manageable number of relevant roles and keep studying. Look at which applications receive replies and how far interviews progress. Avoid drawing firm conclusions from a small sample. If replies stay low, check your targeting and the examples on your resume. If interviews stall, work on the skills or explanations that caused difficulty.

sections.title: Check unfamiliar recruiters and offers
sections.text: Verify the recruiter and opening through the company's official channels. Do not pay to obtain a job or to release supposed earnings. Be careful with unexpected requests for bank details, identity documents, or deposits. A professional-looking website does not prove an offer is genuine. [S4]

checklist: Review the applications and responses you have recorded
Ask for feedback on a specific application or interview
Choose one thing to change next week
